articles.title: Is FireEye Turning Into a Top Cybersecurity Stock?
articles.content: FireEye (NASDAQ: FEYE) has given investors mixed signals over the last few months about where its business is headed as the lack of decent top-line growth has led many to wonder if the company is competitive enough to cut its teeth in the thriving cybersecurity industry. In the second quarter, revenue from FireEye's on-premise product and related subscriptions was down 12% year over year. That might not change as soon as investors hope, given that business still accounts for a significant portion of FireEye's total revenue, which is why investors are likely better off looking to other cybersecurity stocks that are doing a better job of tapping into the end-market opportunity.

articles.title: Cybersecurity Is Quickly Changing in a Work-From-Home World, Writes CrowdStrike CEO
articles.content: Cloud computing has been adopted at a rapid pace, and employees are accessing company data remotely -- thus the need for CrowdStrike's cloud-based endpoint security software, sending its sales (and stock price) through the roof. The small $96 million takeover ($86 million in cash, $10 million in stock) will add further capabilities to the CrowdStrike platform and increase the company's total addressable market (there will be about $2 billion in 2020 global spending on identity security services). The deal for Preempt doesn't exactly stomp on any toes in this alliance, but Kurtz and company clearly understand that more than just securing endpoints will be needed if CrowdStrike wants to create an enduring growth story.
